issues.title: Passenger-side cowl seal leak floods blower motor and floor pan
issues.description:
A very common problem on 90-93 Integras where, after many years, the foam seals beneath the windshield cowl no longer keep water out and it ends up on the passenger floor after passing through the blower motor and rusting it out.
 
The drainage paths beneath the cowl are very shallow and are easily clogged with accumulated dust and leaf matter; one drainage path runs right over the hole where the blower sucks in air, so if there is a blockage downstream rainwater pours right into the blower assembly.
 Drivers see soaked passenger carpet, foggy windshield, musty smell, and eventually a dead blower motor or resistor.
issues.solution:
Order eight of Honda part number 91608-SJ6-003 (the clear grommet/seal pieces) from a Honda or Acura dealer — they are inexpensive at roughly $2.50 each.
 Remove the wiper arms (14mm) and the black plastic cowl, clear out all leaf debris from the drainage channels, then replace the old foam strip with new urethane weatherstripping and reinstall with the new grommets. 
Remove the wipers, pop the 7-8 pins, undo the pins along the perimeter under the hood, clean out the drainage paths, scrape out the old weather stripping, and replace with 1/4" wide, 1/2" thick urethane weather stripping for a permanent fix.
 If the blower motor or resistor has already corroded, replace those at the same time.
symptoms: Wet passenger-side floor mat after rain
Water sprays from vents when blower is turned on
Musty/mildew interior smell
Foggy windshield that won't clear
Blower motor dead or noisy
Rusted blower motor housing

citations.title: DIY: Fixing The Passenger Side Cowl Leak On A 90-93 Integra — Honda-Tech

communityRecommendations.content: Order 8x Honda P/N 91608-SJ6-003 grommets before starting — they're cheap (~$2.50 each) and you'll destroy the originals on removal.
If the blower has been getting wet for a while, plan on also replacing the blower motor and the resistor — water corrodes both.

issues.title: Rear quarter panel and rocker panel rust-through behind wheel arch protectors
issues.description:
Any Integra that still has the rear wheel arch protectors is already starting to rust, even if not visible on the outside — pulling a protector typically reveals wet mud trapped against the inner arch lip with rust eating the metal underneath.
 
This is one of the most common problems on 90's Hondas; it happens on Integras, Civics and Preludes, and the rust bubbles up around the bumper bolt area requiring it to be ground or cut out.
 Owners in salt-belt and humid regions see bubbling paint at the rear wheel arch lip, holes through rocker panels, and structural rust that fails safety inspection.
issues.solution:
All G2 Integras came with rear wheel arch protectors — pull them off as preventive maintenance; Acura wanted around $40-$50 each for them new.
 For early rust, cut out affected metal with at least one inch of clean margin, treat the inner frame with a rust converter such as POR-15, and weld in patch panels (92-95 Civic patch panels can be modified to fit). 
Proper repair is to replace the complete rear quarter — body shop estimates run around $4000 for both sides with paint; DIY gutting/stripping can drop it closer to $2000-$3500.
 Aftermarket wheel arch and quarter patch panels are available from Mill Supply and other restoration vendors.
symptoms: Paint bubbling at rear wheel arch lip
Holes visible in rocker panel behind side skirt
Rust bubbling around rear bumper bolt area
Wet mud/debris trapped behind plastic arch protectors
Fails safety/MOT inspection

communityRecommendations.content: Remove the plastic rear wheel-arch protectors and clean out trapped mud as soon as you buy the car — that's where the rust starts.
Bondo-over is cosmetic only — structural rust on rockers will fail safety inspection and continue to spread.

issues.title: PGM-FI main relay solder joint cracks cause hot-weather no-start
issues.description:
The PGM-FI Main Relay is a critical electronic switch that sends power to the fuel pump and engine computer (ECU); when you turn the key it clicks on, allowing the pump to build pressure and the computer to manage the engine — without a working main relay the engine won't get fuel or the electronic commands it needs to run.
 
The main relay is a known weak point — over many years the solder joints inside the relay crack from heat and vibration, and the problem is often worse on hot days or after the car has been running, as heat causes the cracked joints to expand and lose connection.
 Symptoms include crank-but-no-start after the car sits in the sun, intermittent stalling, and the fuel pump failing to prime audibly when the key is turned to ON.
issues.solution:
Replacing the main relay is one of the easiest repairs on the Integra; it sits under the driver's-side dash to the left of the steering column, held by a single 10mm bolt — unbolt, unplug, plug in the new one.
 
Use a quality replacement (OEM part numbers 39400-SH3-003 or 39400-SH3-A01, or cross-references like Standard Motors RY134 / Bosch 0332019150 / BWD R3128); expect to pay $25-$70 and avoid the cheapest generic relays — reliability matters.
 
Resoldering the cracked joints on the existing relay's circuit board has been done successfully by many owners, but requires skill with a soldering iron and may not be permanent — a new aftermarket relay is the more reliable repair.
symptoms: Engine cranks but won't start when hot
No fuel pump prime sound at key-on
Intermittent stalling while driving
Restarts fine after cooling down
Check engine light may not flash codes if relay is dead

communityRecommendations.content: Carry a spare main relay in the glove box — they're small and a roadside swap can save a tow.
Diagnose first: turn key to ON and listen for the 2-second fuel pump prime. No prime + no audible relay click = main relay.

issues.title: Valve cover gasket and spark plug tube seals leak oil into plug wells
issues.description:
When oil is on top of the spark plug (visible when the boots are removed), it is the spark plug tube seals — they need to be replaced along with the valve cover gasket and exhaust cam seal cap while the cover is off.
 
It's very normal for these grommets to leak on a Honda; oil gets into the spark plug wells and the fix is to take the valve cover off and replace them.
 Drivers notice oil seeping down the sides of the head, oil-soaked spark plug boots, and sometimes misfires if oil shorts the plug wires.
issues.solution:
Buy a valve cover gasket KIT from the dealer and replace all the rubber parts in the bag — the kit contains all the rubber gaskets including the spark plug tube seals; apply a small dab of Hondabond in the corners where the gasket passes over the cam.
 Remove the valve cover, clean the head and cover thoroughly, install the new gasket, four new spark plug tube seals/grommets, and a new half-moon cam seal cap. Torque the valve cover nuts in sequence to spec (around 7-9 ft-lb / 86 in-lb). DIY parts run $20-$60 (Fel-Pro or OEM Honda); shop labor typically adds $150-$300. While the cover is off it's also a good time to do a valve adjustment.
symptoms: Oil pooled in spark plug wells
Oil seeping from sides of valve cover
Burning oil smell at idle
Oil-saturated spark plug boots
Occasional misfire from oil-contaminated plug

citations.title: oil on sparkplug!! — Honda-Acura.net

communityRecommendations.content: Always replace the four spark plug tube grommets and the half-moon cam seal cap at the same time as the main gasket — they're in the kit and old ones won't reseal.
Use a B20/CRV valve cover gasket kit from Honda — it's the same part and often easier to source than the dealer Acura listing.

issues.title: Motorized passive shoulder belt sticks on track or fails to move
issues.description:
US-market 1990-1993 Integras used a motorized passive shoulder belt that travels on a track from the A-pillar to the B-pillar. 
A common failure has the auto belt stuck in the down/forward position with the warning light staying on; pulling it back manually doesn't help because once the door is opened and closed it goes back down but won't return.
 
Symptoms include intermittent retraction — sometimes 100%, sometimes 0%, sometimes stopping partway — accompanied by a constant error beep indicating a seatbelt malfunction.
 Failure modes include blown 30A passive-motor fuses, broken door-jamb switches, worn track gears, and seized motors.
issues.solution:
The seat-belt fuses are under the hood on the passenger-side shock tower — the fuse-box cover labels them; pull and inspect the passive motor L and R fuses (30A each) first.
 
Manually unstick the belt by locating the rod with a hex-head fitting on the motor, then use a screwdriver/Allen key to drive the seat-belt motor manually to the rear position before closing the door.
 
American Acura/Honda has a policy of offering a lifetime warranty on the functional components of their seat belts — as long as the vehicle is an American-market car, has not been in a collision, and the belt assembly has not been modified, American Acura will fix it at their cost; if the dealer refuses, phone Acura Client Relations at (800) 382-2238.
 Note that Honda Canada does not honor this policy.
symptoms: Shoulder belt stuck in forward (door) position
Belt fails to return when door closes
Constant warning chime/beep
Seat belt warning light stays on
Motor audibly hums but belt doesn't move
Belt retracts only intermittently

Do NOT disable the passive belt and rely only on the lap belt — the lap-only belt was never intended as a standalone restraint and offers poor upper-body protection.

issues.title: Outer CV joint boot tears leading to joint failure and clicking
issues.description:
The CV joints are lubricated with grease and sealed inside rubber boots that hold the grease in and keep dirt out; over time the boots crack or tear, grease escapes and dirt enters the joint causing it to break down, and the joint develops excessive play in its bearings, producing a repetitive clicking sound when accelerating through a curve.
 
Clicking or popping noise when turning is the classic sign of a worn outer CV joint, most obvious during sharp low-speed turns like in a parking lot; vibrations while accelerating and dark heavy grease splattered on the inner edge of the tire are additional symptoms.
 Common on the B18A1-powered DA chassis where the outer boots crack with age and especially after donuts in reverse or hard cornering.
issues.solution:
If the boot has just torn and no elements got into the joint, regreasing and rebooting can work — a $10 boot kit vs. a $60 replacement axle is the tradeoff.
 
Reman axles run around $50 each and boot kits about $25 — AutoZone and similar carry both for the 1992 Integra 1.8L DOHC.
 
Pack outer CV joint boot with molybdenum disulfide grease, lube the spider and inside bore of rollers, ensure rollers are aligned with marks made at disassembly and install with the high side of rollers facing outward.
 Use new boot clamps (low-profile metal bands included in kit). Most owners simply swap the full reman half-shaft for under $100/side — quicker than rebooting. Always replace the axle nut and use a new transaxle retaining ring.
symptoms: Clicking or popping when turning at low speed
Grease splattered on inner wheel and suspension
Clunk on acceleration or shifting into gear
Vibration at highway speed
Torn or cracked outer boot visible at full lock

communityRecommendations.content: Inspect both outer boots at every oil change — catching a tear early lets you reboot for $25 instead of replacing the axle.
DA Integras use a dynamic damper (weight) on the axle shaft — make sure any replacement half-shaft includes it or transfer the original.

issues.title: Rear wheel bearing hum from press-in hub assembly
issues.description:
The wheel bearings on the 1986-1993 Acura Integra are critical parts located inside the wheel hub assembly — for the first-generation Integra these are press-in style bearings pressed into the steering knuckle in the front and the hub assembly in the rear, and they support the full weight of the car while it's in motion.
 
When a wheel bearing starts to go bad it usually gives warning signs; ignoring them can lead to serious problems including the wheel separating from the car, and the most common sign is a humming, rumbling, or grinding sound that gets louder with speed.
 
The hum is often hard to localize from inside the cabin — passengers in the back may each think it's on their side — but it typically goes away when steering loads the bad bearing's opposite side.
issues.solution:
This is an advanced DIY job — removing the knuckle from the car is straightforward for a home mechanic, but the bearing itself must be pressed out of the knuckle and the new one pressed in using a hydraulic shop press; without a press take the knuckle to a machine shop.
 Rear bearings on the DA are also press-in (unlike the bolt-on hubs on later 1994+ Integras), so both axles require press work. Quality replacement brands include SKF, Timken, FAG, Koyo and NSK (the latter two are often OEM suppliers to Honda). 
Rear bearings are a bit more expensive but easier to access than the fronts.
 Budget $40-$90 per bearing plus press/labor; total shop cost typically $200-$450 per corner.
symptoms: Humming or rumbling noise that increases with speed
Noise changes pitch or volume when turning
Vibration through floor at highway speed
Slight wheel play when rocked on jack stands
Uneven inner tire wear

communityRecommendations.content: Diagnose by steering side-to-side at highway speed: if the hum lessens when steering right, the bad bearing is on the left (unloaded) side.
Stick with Koyo or NSK bearings — they were the original Honda OEM suppliers and outlast most cheap aftermarket kits.
